See the new facial reconstruction of a man from Roman-era Scotland who was decapitated after his death and buried near a Roman fort.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Researchers have virtually reconstructed the face of a man who was decapitated after his death almost 2,000 years ago and then buried near a Roman military fort in Scotland.

While it's unclear why the man was beheaded, other burials hundreds of miles away may offer a clue. A chemical analysis of the man's remains suggests that he grew up in southern Britain. Beheading bodies may have been an obscure burial rite for some southern Britons, as other decapitated bodies from about the same time have been found in that region, John H. Reid, an archaeologist at the Trimontium Trust who was not involved in the excavations, told Live Science.

Another mystery is why a southern Briton was on the Roman frontier, but it seems that he was working for the Roman army when he died, researchers at National Museums Scotland said in a statement. However, his skeleton shows the man's right arm had such limited movement that he could not have used a sword, so he was probably not a soldier, they added.

Despite this disability, however, it's possible that the man used weapons in his other hand, or had a job in the Roman army that did not require frontline fighting, such as a clerk.

"He could have been left-handed, or he could have had a 'desk job'," said Reid, who is the author of the book "The Eagle and the Bear: A New History of Roman Scotland" (Birlinn, 2023).

The man was probably about 50 years old when he died between A.D. 142 and 165. His remains were then buried near the Roman fort at Inveresk, on Scotland's east coast just southeast of what's now Edinburgh, according to the statement.

An analysis of the man's skeleton indicated that he had lived an active life. His nose had been broken and healed, and his right elbow showed extensive bone growth, perhaps from arthritis. Reid said the bone growth may have been his body's response to a physical injury.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Researchers at National Museums Scotland and the independent U.K.-based forensic anthropologist Christopher Rynn created the facial construction based on the man's skull.

The facial reconstruction is based on the shape of the man's skull. He is shown here without a beard, which was based on what was common at this time.

The Roman fort at Inveresk was built around A.D. 140 and acted as a command-and-supply center for Roman forts along the Antonine Wall, which ran along the shortest route between Scotland's west coast and east coast — roughly the line between Glasgow and Edinburgh, although neither city existed at the time.

The Romans had hoped to secure all of Scotland under their rule after their invasion of Britain under Emperor Claudius in A.D. 43. They tried to impose control after their victory against a coalition of native Caledonian tribes at the Battle of Mons Graupius (possibly near the Scottish city of Perth) in about 83. But by about 120, the Romans had retreated to the heavily fortified line of Hadrian's Wall, near the modern border of England and Scotland.

The fort at Inveresk was built for a second push that aimed to secure Roman control over southern Scotland by establishing the Antonine Wall. But this failed too, and after A.D. 162, the Romans withdrew again to Hadrian's Wall, until the final collapse of Roman rule in Britain in the early fifth century.

Jess Turner, an osteoarchaeologist at National Museums Scotland, with the skull of the man buried outside the Roman fort at Inveresk.

Reid told Live Science that Scotland's soil seldom preserved human skeletons, making the discovery of a Roman-era burial an uncommon find. Although the man had been decapitated after his death, other aspects of his grave indicated he was buried with dignity. In other words, his burial was unlike those of executed criminals, who were often decapitated in Roman-era Britain, he said.

The remains from six Roman-era burials have been found at Inveresk, and four of the dead had been similarly beheaded, the statement said.

There are several ways non-Romans could have served with the Roman army, Reid told Live Science. They might have been employed as servants or artisans attached to the Roman legions, or they might have been soldiers in Roman auxiliary units or even citizen-based legions, he said. By the time of the Antonine Wall, few members of the Roman army in Scotland would have been from the Italian peninsula, he added.

The chemical analysis looked at the ratios of isotopes, or variations of chemical elements, in the man's remains. This analysis suggested that the man had grown up in southern Britain. Alternatively, he may have been recruited from a nearby region, such as the coast of what's now the Netherlands, that gave the same isotopic profile, Reid said.

Reid and his colleagues have found extensive evidence of the Roman army at the Burnswark site in southern Scotland, including the deadly whistling sling bullets they used against their "barbarian" foes. Archaeological work there is ongoing.

What do you know about the Empire's conquest of the British Isles? Find out with our Roman Britain quiz!

Tom writes mainly about science, space, archaeology, the Earth and the oceans. He has also written for the BBC, NBC News, National Geographic, Scientific American, Air & Space, and many others.

Instead, for something ready-to-eat, opt for beloved foods with an established fanbase—perhaps one of the editor-loved finds on Goldbelly. Or, if you want to really impress them, high-quality ingredients are sure to inspire their culinary creativity. That’s why my go-to food gift is an olive oil gift set from Enzo’s Table.

The Signature Selection gift set offers a diverse lineup of flavors to impress your favorite foodies.

Folks at Enzo’s Table have been farming their vineyard in California’s fertile San Joaquin Valley for nearly a century. This gives their gourmand products a farm-to-table feel that’s backed by decades of know-how. In fact, over the years, the brand has proudly received over 200 awards for its signature olive oils, jams and biscotti!

The Signature Selection olive oil gift set is a fleet consisting of four of Enzo’s famous olive oils, plus their signature balsamic vinegar. All five 100ml bottles are organic, having been produced in the San Joaquin Valley vineyard. The gift set contains the following:

The Delicate EVOO offers a buttery flavor and incredibly mild yet peppery finish, making it a perfectly smooth pick for dipping bread or incorporating into salad dressings. Enzo’s Basil Crush EVOO is, as you’d expect, herby and earthy. It’s another option that’s particularly good for roasts, especially red meats. I also love adding a splash on caprese salad.

The Traditional Balsamic Vinegar is incredibly versatile in all the ways you love to see with balsamic. I’ve tried a lot of balsamic over the years, and this one might be the thickest, richest blend I’ve enjoyed.

#6680. Bourbon Caramel Apple Pie

The one thing that can make classic apple pie better? Caramel! That it’s laced with a generous dose of bourbon vaults it straight into hall-of-fame territory. Made using a double batch of our never-fail Perfect Pie Crust, this pretty lattice-topped pie is a crowd-pleaser, familiar enough to appeal to the traditionalists with just enough of a surprise from the booze and the smoky burnt sugar to make the thrill-seekers come back for more. Like all good things, apple pie can’t be rushed. It needs time to chill, bake, and rest—so plan ahead, especially if it’s for Thanksgiving.

Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

2 hours 15 minutes (plus 7 hours for chilling and cooling)

Whisk 3⅓ cups (417 g) all-purpose flour, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. baking powder in a large bowl to combine. Add 4 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces; rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 1¼ cups (2½ sticks) chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash with your fingers into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea-size).

Make a well in the center of mixture and pour in ½ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute, then knead in bowl a couple of times to bring dough together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn out dough onto a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour; dust top of dough with flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold dough in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Divide dough in half and pat each piece into a ½"-thick disk. Wrap each disk tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap each disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

Place 1 cup (200 g) granulated sugar and ½ cup water in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot and cover. Bring to a boil over medium heat (no need to stir); cook until sugar is dissolved, 4–7 minutes total. Uncover and continue to cook, stirring or swirling pot occasionally, until caramel turns a deep golden brown, 10–12 minutes.

Add zest of 1 lemon, 3 lb. Honeycrisp apples (about 6 large), peeled, cored, quartered, thinly sliced crosswise, ½ cup bourbon, 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. ground cinnamon to caramel (it may become stiff). Cover and cook, stirring occasionally, until caramel dissolves and apples have released a generous amount of liquid and are tender but still retain their shape (they should look mostly translucent), 15–18 minutes.

Stir ⅓ cup heavy cream, 3 Tbsp. cornstarch, and 2 Tbsp. cool water in a small bowl until cornstarch is dissolved. Pour into apple mixture and cook (it should be bubbling), stirring often, until mixture is thick, about 5 minutes. Transfer filling to a large bowl; let cool. Cover and chill until cold, at least 45 minutes.

Meanwhile, let dough sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Unwrap 1 disk and roll out on a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour to a 12" round, about ¼" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and wrap around rolling pin. Transfer to a 9"-diameter pie pan (such as East Fork Spun Iron Pie Dish). Unfurl into pan, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into pan. Trim, leaving about a 1" overhang. Chill 15 minutes.

Unwrap remaining disk; roll out on surface lightly dusted with more rice flour to a 18x12" rectangle, about ⅛" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and transfer to a large parchment-lined baking sheet. Brush dough with a thin film of cold water; sprinkle remaining ¼ cup (50 g) granulated sugar over and press gently with your hands to cover dough completely in an even layer (coating dough before cutting into strips will give you the most even coverage). Chill 15 minutes.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 375°. Spoon chilled filling into pie pan and smooth surface to level. Using a ruler, cut dough rectangle into 1"-wide strips. Lay 5–8 strips over filling, spacing evenly across surface to cover. Weave another 5–8 strips over, then under, alternating to create a lattice crust (you may not use all of the strips). Trim overhang to match bottom crust. Press edges of top and bottom crusts firmly together to seal, then trim again, leaving about ¼" overhang. Fold overhang up and over lattice so crust is flush with edges of pan and crimp as desired with lightly floured fingers.

Place pan on a rimmed baking sheet (to catch drips) and bake pie until crust is set and golden, 45–50 minutes. Reduce oven temperature to 350°; continue to bake until crust is deep golden brown and filling is bubbling up through lattice, 40–50 minutes more. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let pie cool in pan at least 4 hours before serving.

Do Ahead: Filling can be made 2 days ahead; keep chilled. Pie can be baked 1 day ahead; store, loosely covered, at room temperature.

#6679. BA's Best Orecchiette With Sausage and Broccoli Rabe

Unlike many iconic Italian recipes, this luxurious union of silky broccoli rabe, chile-flecked sausage, garlic, and curvaceous pasta is a weeknight hero. You can make it start to finish, in about 30 minutes. The key to successful execution is to go way beyond blanching when it comes to precooking the broccoli rabe in boiling salted water. For tender rabe that melds seamlessly with pasta and sausage, start by separating the thick stems from the rest of the stalks and giving them a head start before adding the rest. It removes any unpleasant bitterness and also means the rabe will cook into the saucy base of browned sausage and sweated garlic in just minutes.

While orecchiette is the traditional pasta choice, any short pasta will work. Sausage has become a popular addition to the true original Pugliese dish of stewed broccoli rabe with pasta, but a tin of anchovies makes a great substitute for added oomph and intensity.

This recipe is one of BA’s Best, our vault of the Test Kitchen's definitive takes on iconic dishes.

Cut 2 large bunches broccoli rabe, trimmed, in half crosswise to separate thick stalks from thinner stems and florets. Cook thicker stalks in a medium pot of boiling salted water until crisp-tender, about 5 minutes. Add thinner stems and florets and cook until all of the broccoli rabe is tender (the tip of a paring knife should slide through the stalks with little to no resistance), about 3 minutes. Transfer to a rimmed baking sheet with tongs; let sit until cool enough to handle (no need to squeeze out excess water unless dripping wet). Coarsely chop into bite-size pieces.

Meanwhile, cook 1 lb. orecchiette (little ear-shaped pasta) or other short pasta in a second medium pot of boiling salted water until al dente (or use same pot with fresh salted water). Drain, reserving 2 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 1 lb. hot Italian sausage, casings removed if needed, breaking up with a wooden spoon, until golden brown and nearly cooked through, about 5 minutes. Add 1 head of garlic, cloves separated, peeled, thinly sliced, and remaining 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Cook, breaking up sausage even finer if needed and stirring often, until garlic is golden brown and softened, 3–4 minutes. Add broccoli rabe and cook, stirring occasionally, until very tender and wilted, about 5 minutes.

Add 4 Tbsp. (½ stick) unsalted butter, cut into pieces, pasta, and 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Cook, stirring often and adding more pasta cooking liquid as needed, until pasta is coated in a clingy sauce. Taste and add some crushed red pepper flakes if desired. Add 1 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about ½ cup), and stir, adding more pasta cooking liquid a splash at a time as needed to keep sauce smooth and shiny, until incorporated; season with salt.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with more Parmesan.

#6678. Stanley Tucci Reveals His Family's Holiday Tradition That Always Ends In Chaos

The fun starts once everyone stops taking it seriously.

Stanley Tucci has spent years taking audiences on culinary adventures through Italy, so it’s no surprise S.Pellegrino would tap the icon for a holiday collaboration built around the dinner table. Now, he’s teaming up with the brand again, this time on limited-edition S.Pellegrino bottles with labels designed to keep the conversation going even after the meal turns cold.

Tucci has partnered with the brand since 2022, but he’s been a fan for far longer. In fact, he even has a trick for using it in a martini. “If you make a martini on the rocks—vodka martini, gin martini, whatever you want—a little splash of San Pellegrino in it is great,” he shares with me. “It gives it a little lift.”

Cocktails aside, one thing he thinks his fans would be surprised to learn is that the devout coffee drinker sometimes enjoys a cup of rooibos tea. “I find it very comforting, particularly when you’re on set, making a movie. That, with a little bit of honey,” he says of how he enjoys the drink.

His actual holiday traditions can get a little more animated. “Around the holidays, sometimes we’ll play charades with the kids in the evening, and it’s just fun because I don’t like to keep score,” he shares. “The fun part of it is watching people get up and trying to get a point across; it’s hysterical to me.”

It’s the generational divide, though, that really makes him laugh.

“What I love about charades too is when you play with little kids,” he says. “They’ll get upset because they don’t fully understand it—they’ll get upset if you get it quickly, which is sort of the point, because they want to stay up there and keep doing it, as opposed to the adult who just wants it to be over with.”

So while the new S.Pellegrino bottles may get people talking, it’s what unfolds afterward that seems to stick with Tucci most.

His favorite holiday moments are the ones “when people just suddenly start bursting into song, or say, ‘Hey, let’s play charades,’ and then the charades go on forever, all the rules go out the window, and nobody really keeps track of who’s winning or losing,” he says. “That’s the most fun.”

A biology student found a Native American stone spearpoint when searching for shark teeth along the coast of Virginia.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On the last day of an ecology field trip to Virginia's Eastern Shore, a biology undergraduate student discovered more than she expected. While searching for shark teeth, Brooklyn Rolph, a student at Mary Baldwin University in Virginia, stumbled upon a stone spearpoint estimated to be around 4,500 years old.

"Wow, this is so crazy," Rolph said in a statement. Already primed to look for pointy objects underwater, Rolph found a stone spear and immediately alerted the professors running the trip. "They were ecstatic," she recalled.

The stone artifact is about 6 inches (15 centimeters) long and, according to local archaeologists, a type known as a Lehigh/Koens-Crispin point. This kind of stone tool was made by Indigenous people across the East Coast of the U.S. from around 4,500 to 3,000 years ago. Sometimes called a "broadspear," the stone point also may have been used as a knife by prehistoric hunter-gatherers in the Late Archaic period.

The stone point is likely 3,000 to 4,500 years old.

The field trip was part of an ecology course led by Mary Baldwin University faculty members who had secured a permit from the state to explore the barrier islands off the Eastern Shore, the southern part of the Delmarva Peninsula that includes most of Delaware and parts of Virginia and Maryland.

Just after a lunch break on Sept. 21, the last day of the excursion that aimed to let students study plants and animals in the coastal ecosystem, Rolph set out to quickly explore a mound of shells on the island and noticed the spearpoint at the edge of an inlet. Her professors were blown away by the lucky discovery.

"The set of circumstances that came together that made this possible is quite unbelievable," Paul Callo, a biology professor at Mary Baldwin University who was co-leading the trip, said in the statement. "The tide was coming in, so the spear point was soon to be buried."

When Rolph showed Callo the artifact, he was "truly at a loss for words," he said. "It is certainly awe-inspiring to see and touch something that was made by human hands thousands of years ago."

The barrier island where Rolph found the stone point is part of a natural area owned by the Virginia Department of Conservation and Recreation, which means the artifact is now the property of the Commonwealth of Virginia. Archaeologists collected it from the Mary Baldwin group and have taken it to the Virginia Department of Historic Resources for further study.

Rolph was fine with not keeping the spearpoint. "That's how you get cursed!" she said.

How much do you know about the first people to reach the Americas? Find out with our First Americans quiz!

Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.

#6676. Dave & Buster's Is Becoming "Doom & Buster's" With Five New Marvel-Inspired Drinks

New games, new drinks, and plenty of reasons for superhero lovers to stop by.

Dave & Buster's is getting a major makeover, and we have Doctor Doom to thank.

Ahead of Marvel Studios' Avengers: Doomsday, the restaurant and arcade chain is temporarily renaming itself Doom & Buster's as part of a nationwide takeover featuring themed games, exclusive merchandise, and five new drinks. And considering the movie doesn't hit theaters until December 18, fans will have plenty of time to get in on the action beforehand.

New Marvel games and experiences began rolling out November 4, ahead of the full transformation on November 16. That's when participating Dave & Buster's locations will become Doom & Buster's, complete with immersive Doomsday Zones, Marvel-inspired games, collectible Power Cards, and themed prizes. The takeover runs through January 31, 2027, although specific attractions will vary by location.

There's also DOOMHOUR, a surprise hour when D&B Rewards members can earn double tickets on eligible arcade games. Members will receive advance notice through the rewards app.

The chain is introducing three limited-time cocktails and two alcohol-free mocktails, all inspired by Marvel characters and the upcoming movie.

First up is Doomsday's Dominion, which combines Smirnoff vodka, melon liqueur, pineapple, and lemon-lime soda. It also comes with a Black Magic sidecar that guests can pour into the drink themselves.

There's also the Multiversal Mule, made with vodka, blue orange liqueur, dragon fruit, and ginger beer. It comes with edible shimmer and an LED glow cube, so it'll be hard to miss at the bar.

For anyone who can't decide on just one drink, the Fantastic Flight includes four miniature cocktails made with vodka, orange liqueur, and citrus sour, each featuring its own flavor.

The mocktails are getting just as much attention to detail.

Panther's Potion combines cherry, ginger beer, and citrus sour, and comes with a blue shimmer sidecar inspired by vibranium and a silver sugar rim. Meanwhile, Captain Punch mixes blue raspberry, coconut, pineapple, lemon-lime soda, and citrus sour, topped with a blue sugar rim, cherries, and a blue sour candy strip.

All five drinks will be available from November 16 through January 31, 2027.

#6675. I Tried the New AirDoctor 1500 Tower—And It’s the Perfect Size for Eliminating Kitchen Odors

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

It happens to the best of us. You’re minding your own business as dessert bubbles in the oven or dinner sears on the stove, then—bam! The smell of burning reaches your nose, and before you know it, you’re dragging out a stepladder to silence the blaring smoke alarm.

I hate to say that this is a fairly frequent scenario in my kitchen. While I do my best to prevent pans of lasagna from overflowing and exercise caution when searing steak, accidents still occur. The only difference is that I now have a solution to clear the lingering smell from my space.

I’ve been testing the AirDoctor 1500 air purifier for two months, and it’s a portable yet powerful option for eliminating pesky kitchen odors. Here’s everything you need to know.

Banish bad odors from your kitchen with this mini-yet-mighty air purifier.

The AirDoctor 1500 is a high-performance air purifier packed into a sleek, compact package. Unlike other air purifiers that can take up as much space as a dehumidifier, the 1500 measures less than 10 inches wide and 21 inches high. It features three filters: a pre-filter for trapping larger particles like pet hair, a carbon and VOC filter for filtering odors and an UltraHEPA for capturing everything else. It’s best suited for small-to-medium spaces up to 320 square feet and comes in black or white.

I’ve been testing the AirDoctor 1500 air purifier since its launch in September 2026. I’ve used it in my kitchen, entryway, office and family room.

The AirDoctor arrived on my doorstep in a sturdy brown box. It was well-packaged to prevent damage during shipping, and setup couldn’t be easier. All you have to do is lift the unit out of the box, remove the plastic bag, peel off a few stickers and, most importantly, set up the filter.

The filter housing snaps off easily, and installation is as simple as removing the filter from its packaging and popping it back in. In all the air purifiers I’ve tested, AirDoctor has the most seamless filter access, thanks to built-in magnets in the housing. This is important not only for changing the filter but also for cleaning it.

After completing setup, I plugged in the AirDoctor and turned it on. It immediately whirred to life, starting at high speed with a red light and working its way down to a low-speed setting. The control panel is reactive to a simple touch, with options for speed (auto, one, two, three or four), ion, dim and timer. The interface also includes a light that signals when the filter needs to be checked or replaced.

As the air purifier got to work, I was impressed with how little sound it produced. On level one, you can barely hear it. It’s a slightly audible white noise that blends easily into the background. Level four is obviously the loudest, similar to a fan on high speed. If you’re very sensitive to noise, you might find any air purifier, including the AirDoctor, too loud to sleep with. But in a kitchen, the whir blends right into the din of cooking, a running dishwasher and other ambient sounds.

Within a week of the AirDoctor being in my space, it faced its first real challenge. I had a potpie galette in a 425-degree oven, and some of the filling started to leak onto the pizza steel it was baking on and burn. Within minutes, my oven filled with smoke. I managed to get the galette out without setting off the alarms, but my space was filled with an unpleasant, burning-vegetable odor.

I turned on the AirDoctor, set it to auto, and it immediately kicked into high gear. The light turned red—a sign that it senses poor air quality—and the fan worked overtime to cleanse the air. After about 15 minutes, the light turned yellow—moderate air quality—and I could already sense a difference. Within an hour, it was back to a blue light, which signifies good air quality, and it’s like the accident never happened.

Over the next few weeks, the AirDoctor helped clear the air after I burnt some toast in the toaster and cooked cruciferous vegetables. It also helps combat day-to-day odors, like a full trash can or a garbage disposal ready for a scrubdown.

What I like best is that the AirDoctor isn’t just masking these scents; it’s actually removing them from the air. As an allergy sufferer, I’ve also noticed fewer symptoms (especially sneezing) when the air purifier is running. Thanks to the 1500’s portable size, it’s easy to tote it around my downstairs living area, too.

The AirDoctor’s filters are designed to last—but the exact lifespan depends on many factors. How long you run the air purifier each day, for starters. Along with what kind of baseline air quality is in your home. Pets, for example, are an obvious culprit for added dander and hair. Luckily, the 1500 includes a built-in sensor light that tells you when it’s time for a refresh.

You can also pop off the housing and give the filter a good vacuum. I like to do this once a month or so, but again, buildup may be more or less severe depending on your home’s air quality conditions.

I’ve had the opportunity to also test the AirDoctor 1500’s larger cousin, the AirDoctor 3500. But how do these models compare?

Size is the most obvious difference. The 1500 is six inches slimmer than the 3500 and weighs roughly half as much. I find that the 1500 blends more seamlessly into my space than the 3500, taking up less footprint. The round tower design is also very easy to slip into a corner.

That said, the 1500 covers rooms up to 320 sq. ft., while the 3500 covers up to 630 sq. ft. This makes the 1500 a great option for kitchens, offices, laundry rooms and small bedrooms, while the 3500 is a better choice for large living rooms and open-concept homes.

Beyond that, performance is very similar. Both models are quiet and easy to operate. They use a 3-stage filtration system, including an UltraHEPA. They’re both high-quality machines that are built to last. And that quality does come at a premium. The 1500 retails for $399, while the 3500 costs $659.

My spouse likes to joke that I’m like a basset hound given how sensitive I am to smells. That’s why the AirDoctor 1500 is an obvious choice in our kitchen. It efficiently rids our space of odors from cooking, pungent foods and even the occasional smoke-induced accident. Not only is this machine reducing odors that would otherwise linger for days, but it’s also cleansing our air of other contaminants.

This way to cleaner air! I love this air purifier's slim footprint, low noise level and triple filter design.

The AirDoctor 1500 air purifier is available from the brand’s website or Amazon. It retails for $399.

#6674. BA’s Best Green Bean Casserole With Step-by-Step Video

This green bean casserole recipe skips the canned soup. Chris Morocco’s take on the classic Thanksgiving side pairs fresh green beans and deeply browned crimini mushrooms with a garlicky Parmesan béchamel. As for the topping, French’s fried onions are iconic for good reason, and they are staying right where they belong.

Give the mushrooms room to brown, salt the blanching water generously (like you would for cooking pasta), and taste the mushrooms and sauce before assembling. As written, you can cook the mushrooms and make the sauce at the same time. To save a pan, cook the mushrooms first, then transfer them to a plate and make the béchamel in the same pan, scraping up all the browned bits.

For the rest of the spread, turn to our classic Thanksgiving menu →

Can I make green bean casserole ahead of time?

Yes. Blanch the green beans, cook the mushrooms, and make the sauce up to 1 day ahead; cool and refrigerate them separately. Assemble and bake the day you plan to serve it, adding the fried onions during the final few minutes of baking.

We don’t recommend freezing the assembled casserole—the cream sauce can separate, and the beans turn mushy after thawing and reheating.

How do I keep the cream sauce from separating?

Don’t overreduce it. Once the béchamel is thick and bubbling, take it off the heat before whisking in the garlic and Parmesan. Boiling off too much liquid can cause the fat to separate. Stick with the recipe’s amount of Parmesan, too—extra cheese can contribute to a broken sauce.

Blanched, fresh beans are our first choice, but readers have reported success with frozen petite and French-cut beans. We haven’t tested the swap, but recommend thawing them overnight in your refrigerator and straining the excess liquid before continuing.

Can I make this green bean casserole gluten-free?

We haven’t tested a gluten-free version, but our editors suggest replacing the all-purpose flour with a gluten-free flour blend. You’ll also need to seek out gluten-free fried onions, or try our flourless Crispy Fried Shallots.

Place rack in middle of oven; preheat oven to 375°. Working in batches, cook 2 lb. fresh green beans in a large pot of boiling salted water until bright green and halfway to tenderness, about 3 minutes per batch. Drain and let cool; trim stem ends.

Heat 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Cook ½ lb. crimini mushrooms, sliced, without stirring, until golden brown underneath, about 2 minutes. Toss and continue to cook, tossing occasionally, until browned on both sides, about 3 minutes more. Add 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter and 2 large thyme sprigs to pan. Cook, tossing occasionally, until butter browns and mushrooms are dark brown and very tender, about 4 minutes longer. Season with kosher salt and transfer to a plate. Repeat with 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter, salt, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, ½ lb. crimini mushrooms, sliced, and 2 large thyme sprigs.

Melt remaining 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large saucepan over medium-low. Whisk in 2 Tbsp. all-purpose flour and cook, whisking occasionally, until roux is golden brown and smells mildly nutty, about 4 minutes. Whisk in 1¼ cups whole milk and 1 cup heavy cream. Increase heat and bring to a simmer, whisking often, and cook until béchamel sauce is thick and bubbling, about 5 minutes. Remove from heat and whisk in 4 garlic cloves, finely grated, and ½ cup grated Parmesan; season with salt and freshly ground pepper.

Arrange green beans and mushrooms in a 2-qt. baking dish. Pour sauce over bean mixture (it may not look like enough, but it will get saucier as it bakes). Cover tightly with foil and bake until sauce is bubbling, 25–30 minutes. Uncover and continue to bake until casserole is lightly browned on top and around the edges, 15–20 minutes longer. Top with ¾ cup French’s fried onions and continue to bake just until onions are slightly darker and fragrant, about 3 minutes. Let sit 10 minutes to set before serving.

#6673. A Beautiful Cabbage Galette

Cut this festive galette into little squares for a hearty appetizer, or serve sizeable wedges as a vegetarian main or standout side. It’s worth seeking out savoy cabbage, the ruffly sort that looks like lace. Ordinary green cabbage, which has a higher moisture content and flatter texture, doesn’t work here (we tried).

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Whisk 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, ¼ tsp. baking powder, and 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour in a large bowl. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces, and rub in with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea size). Make a well in the center and pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute. Knead dough in bowl just to bring together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn dough out onto a lightly dusted surface and sprinkle with all-purpose flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting dough with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

When dough is almost done chilling, cut 1 medium head of savoy cabbage (1¾–2¼ lb.) in half and cut out triangular core at bottom; discard. Separate leaves and tear into pieces about the size of your palm. Transfer about half to a large bowl and set aside.

Melt 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add 1 medium white or yellow onion, thinly sliced, and season generously with kosher salt. Cook, stirring occasionally, until softened and starting to turn translucent, about 5 minutes. Add remaining 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter and ¾ tsp. cumin seeds (if using) and cook until butter is melted. Add remaining cabbage leaves and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion is translucent and lightly browned and cabbage is wilted, 18–22 minutes. Transfer to a large plate or a small baking sheet; chill in fridge or freezer until cool.

Place a rack in bottom third of oven; preheat to 400°. Whisk 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, ⅓ cup heavy cream, 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a measuring glass to combine. Pour cream mixture over reserved raw cabbage leaves and toss with your hands to coat. Add 5 oz. Gruyère or sharp cheddar, coarsely grated, and toss again to combine.

Unwrap dough and roll out on a lightly floured sheet of parchment paper to a 13–14" round (some dough will extend beyond the parchment). Transfer on parchment paper to a baking sheet.

Spread cooked cabbage mixture over dough, leaving about a 1½" border around edges. Fold dough up and over filling, folding and tucking as needed to make a rustic border. Pile raw cabbage mixture on top of cooked cabbage mixture to make a dramatic heap. (It will look ridiculously high at first but will cook down when it bakes.)

Bake galette 25 minutes. Rotate baking sheet front to back, reduce heat to 375°, and bake until cabbage and crust are deep golden brown, 25–35 minutes. (If cabbage seems to be browning too much, reduce heat to 350° toward the end.) Let galette cool on baking sheet at least 1 hour and up to 4 hours before serving.

Do Ahead: Sautéed cabbage can be made 1 day ahead. Transfer to an airtight container and chill. Tightly wrap undressed raw cabbage in plastic and chill.

#6672. Chrissy Teigen Opens Up About First Christmas Without Her Dad: ‘I Don’t Exactly Know What To Expect’

The holiday will bring a mix of joy and sadness as she honors her father through family traditions.

Chrissy Teigen is known for her candid, filter-free personality and playful, unpretentious comfort food, especially around the holidays. But this Christmas will be different. In an exclusive interview with Delish, the cookbook author shares how she's preparing for her first holiday season without her dad.

Teigen announced the death of her father, Ron Teigen Sr., over the summer in an emotional Instagram post, per People. “Yesterday I woke up with a daddy and went to bed without one,” Teigen wrote in her caption.

In the caption, she described the shock of losing him in the middle of an otherwise ordinary day.

“All the same things happened. Hurried shower. Picked up stuffing from the dog toys. Answered some emails. Avoided some. Laughed with my friends and put on a pretty dress for a friend's birthday. Took a video. How cute is this dress!” she continued. “And then my dad just like...f---ing died.”

She admitted that she wasn’t prepared for how hard the loss would hit.

“I thought that since we talk about it and I’ve come to terms with him always having been an ‘old dad’ that I wouldn't have fallen to the ground the way I did. I’ve thought about this phone call for years. I’ll be ready,” she wrote.

This will be her first Christmas without her father, and Chrissy says it will be emotionally complicated.

“[Christmas] will be filled with so much joy, but it’s going to be an emotional one for me, of course. To have that big yellow chair that my dad loved so much, empty...I don’t exactly know what to expect from me emotionally, but I can imagine it will be all the things that make the holidays so complex: sad and wonderful and special all at the same time.”

Chrissy plans to pay tribute to her dad in part by cooking the scalloped potatoes her family makes every year. “We will bake, with love, the potatoes Dad loved so, so much.”

Chrissy also reflects on other family members they have lost. John Legend’s grandmother, Marjorie Maxine Stephen, passed away in 2021 at 91. “We will clean the greens the way Granny (on John’s side) told us to. I’m sure our eyes will well up. It’ll be a testament to how much they meant to us all.”

John and Chrissy share four children—Luna, 10, Miles, 8, Esti, 3, and Wren, 3—and are looking forward to staying home for the holidays. The kids will have time to participate in one of the family’s favorite activities: crafting. “I wanted to stay home for the holidays this year because I need all my children to start hand-making their ornaments and putting them on the tree,” Chrissy says.

“I’ve entered this time in my life where I want Christmas to be completely whimsical and over the top. I want to have a cute, colorful, chaotic Christmas this year.”

The Vera C. Rubin Observatory has found what might be a new dwarf planet in our solar system, orbiting the sun on an inclined plane past Pluto.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Vera C. Rubin Observatory has found what might be a tiny new world in the far reaches of our solar system, hidden beyond the orbit of Neptune — and it is among the largest and brightest objects ever discovered beyond Neptune.

If confirmed, the miniature world would increase the number of officially recognized solar system dwarf planets to six. Upper estimates of the object's size place it at more than half the diameter of Pluto, the largest known dwarf planet.

"My first reaction was one of excited disbelief," Matthew Holman, an astrophysicist at the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory and member of the Rubin team who wrote the code that helped discover the prospective dwarf planet, said in a statement. "Objects like this are very rare, so I immediately started checking whether I or the code had done something wrong."

The potential dwarf planet, designated 2026 ED138, orbits the sun at roughly 46 times the distance between Earth and the sun. The potential new planetoid has been hiding behind galactic camouflage; with its orbit tilted at a 25-degree angle from the solar system plane, it's at just the right angle to get lost in the light from the inner Milky Way, the researchers said.

Many telescopes struggle to see past the millions of stars making up our galaxy's bulge. The Vera C. Rubin Observatory, however, images the entire southern sky every few nights with the largest digital camera ever built, sending out millions of nightly alerts for every object that has changed brightness or position. This makes it exceptional at identifying anything that moves, from solar system objects to transient events like supernova explosions.

The observatory had only just begun its 10-year mission of scanning the sky in July, and ED138 stood out in the data.

Holman works on the software algorithms that process the extreme amounts of data the observatory collects. The code he developed with his colleague, Kevin Napier, compares billions of observations to determine which ones are detections of the same moving object. Running data from Rubin through the code revealed the unusually large object.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

By looking at past data from Rubin and archival images from the Dark Energy Camera mounted on the Victor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope at Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory (both in Chile), the team was able to map out ED138's orbit over the past 10 years.

The Kuiper Belt is a region of the solar system beyond Neptune that is a wild frontier of small, mostly icy bodies made from frozen methane, ammonia, water and rock. It ranges from roughly 30 to 50 times the distance between Earth and the sun, and is home to most of the known dwarf planets, including Pluto. Thousands of Kuiper Belt objects have already been discovered. These space rocks can be frozen time capsules that hold clues about the early solar system's formation.

A model of the solar system showing the five dwarf planets officially recognized by the International Astronomical Union (IAU) and the orbit of the newly discovered dwarf planet candidate 2026 ED138.

Dwarf planets are the largest Kuiper Belt objects that we know of. Bigger than asteroids but not quite planets, dwarf planets are big enough to be rounded under the force of their own gravity but too small to clear their orbits like planets do. While the International Astronomical Union (IAU) has officially confirmed five dwarf planets — Pluto, Ceres, Eris, Haumea and Makemake — astronomers studying dwarf planets often recognize at least nine, with several more candidates whose properties are still unknown.

Depending on which astronomer you ask, there could be anywhere from a handful to hundreds of dwarf planets in this part of the solar system. Identifying which Kuiper Belt objects are dwarf planets is tricky because they are often very dim and move very slowly from Earth's perspective, since their orbits are so large and distant. The likeliest candidates have high albedo (surface reflectivity) and diameters greater than roughly 370 to 500 miles (600 to 800 km).

What makes ED138 special is its size, inferred from its brightness, albedo and distance from the sun. It's estimated to have a diameter between 370 to 930 miles (600 to 1,500 km). For comparison, Pluto — the largest dwarf planet recognized by the IAU — is 1,477 miles (2,377 km) in diameter. Ceres, the smallest IAU-recognized dwarf planet, is 595 miles (958 km) in diameter. Future observations of ED138 will give researchers a more accurate idea of its diameter and density to determine if it's round enough to join the dwarf planet club.

"If confirmed as a dwarf planet, ED138 would join a very small family of worlds," Holman said in the statement. "Rubin will image the whole southern sky again and again for ten years, so any others hiding in the places earlier surveys skipped are now within reach."

Damien Pine (he/him) is a freelance writer, artist, and former NASA engineer. He writes about science, physics, tech, art, and other topics with a focus on making complicated ideas accessible. He has a degree in mechanical engineering from the University of Connecticut, and he gets really excited every time he sees a cat.

#6669. Pear Salad With Honey-Roasted Seeds

In the midst of a rich meal, something fresh and acidic keeps your taste buds awake. Where lettuce splashed with vinaigrette can feel like an afterthought, a juicy, savory-slanting pear salad is worth making room for on a plate full of turkey and cornbread. This is the antithesis of the haphazardly chunked together fruit salads you find at the supermarket for a brunch or dessert spread. Keep the focus on crisp-tart pears—apples also work—and it’s a welcome accompaniment to the other hearty dishes. Sliced razor-thin (use a mandoline) and fanned out on a platter, the fruit acts as an edible canvas for wisps of cheese and clusters of honey-roasted seeds. Leftovers (if you have any, of course) are delightful spooned over a well-toasted and buttered slice of multigrain bread the next day.

Pick firm green pears (Bartlett and Anjou are fair game; use Asian pears in a pinch) to ensure they hold their shape once sliced—even a little underripe is better than slightly over. After slicing, have a taste: If they are very tart, add 1 tsp. honey to the dressing; if fairly sweet, skip it.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Preheat oven to 325°. Whisk 3 Tbsp. honey, 1 tsp. garlic powder, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, and ¾ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl to combine. Add 1 cup raw sunflower seeds, pumpkin seeds (pepitas), and/or coarsely crushed raw nuts (such as walnuts, almonds, and/or hazelnuts) and stir to coat. Spread out in a single layer on a parchment-lined rimmed baking sheet; reserve bowl.

Bake seed mixture until golden brown, 12–14 minutes. (Honey mixture will puff up a bit but will deflate when you stir.) Toss honey-roasted seeds, then let cool. Toss again just to break up.

Whisk 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice, 1 tsp. Dijon mustard, a pinch of kosher salt, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in reserved bowl. Add 2 lb. firm green pears (such as Bartlett and/or Anjou; about 4 large), cored, thinly sliced, to dressing and gently toss to coat.

Arrange pears on a large flat platter. Scatter honey-roasted seeds over and top with 2 oz. Parmesan, aged white cheddar, or Manchego cheese, shaved.

Do Ahead: Honey-roasted seeds can be made 6 hours ahead. Store at room temperature.

#6668. For Talarico and Hinojosa, Whataburger Is a Perfectly Texas Place to Celebrate

Like so many Texans on so many nights, Senator-elect James Talarico and Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa ended their evening at Whataburger.

Late Tuesday night, after Talarico flipped a Senate seat for the Democrats and Hinojosa was elected the first Democratic governor of the state in more than three decades, the two sat down at an Austin-area location of Whataburger, the iconic regional fast food chain, to clink plastic orange-and-white-striped cups.

It was a fitting setting for the pair, who played critical roles in the blue wave that swept the country in the midterm elections on Tuesday night. Talarico, who defeated scandal-plagued Republican Ken Paxton, went on the offensive against billionaires, prevailing with a positive, populist message against a party funded by Elon Musk and other ultrawealthy donors.

Hinojosa, the first Latina to be elected governor for Texas, targeted corruption and data centers in her race against Republican incumbent Greg Abbott. Both Talarico and Hinojosa will be the first Democrats in more than 30 years to serve Texas in their respective roles.

But even in the midst of a polarizing political moment for the nation, loving Whataburger is bigger than politics in Texas. Since opening its first location in Corpus Christi, Texas, in 1950, the chain, with its signature A-frame buildings, has become a social center for small towns, a place for a budget-friendly meal for families, and a crucial hangout for high schoolers figuring out where else they’ll go that night or stopping for a late-night breakfast before heading home.

Instead of popping Champagne, it’s poignant that Talarico and Hinojosa celebrated with oversize sodas. You can still get a double-burger Whatameal for under $15. These aren't the first Democrats to harness the tangy-sweet appeal of Whataburger's much-beloved Fancy Ketchup. In 2018, the campaign for senate-hopeful Beto O'Rourke shared video of him skateboarding outside a Whataburger before going inside to eat.

Today’s prices are squarely in line with the affordability politics that resonated with voters this cycle. And Talarico and Hinojosa’s Whataburger cheers was a fitting end to a campaign that wove food and politics together. While casting himself as a David against Paxton’s Goliath, Talarico absorbed attacks that claimed he was vegan. While the Senator-elect had urged residents to cut down on beef consumption, he denied the dietary restriction, countering by posting pictures of himself chowing down on barbecue.

Paxton still tried to label his opponent as “Tofu Talarico,” and Trump imagined a scenario where Talarico excuses himself to vomit after eating meat. The barbs were not-so-subtle assaults on Talarico’s manhood, the latest manifestation of the link between meat and masculinity. But there was Talarico on election night, sitting in the house of beef patties, Whatachick’n strips, and bacon-and-egg taquitos.

After a 2019 acquisition by a Chicago-based investment firm, Whataburger has faced allegations of diminishing quality and a nascent rival in Austin’s P. Terry’s Burger Stand. And still, aside from a Dairy Queen or A&W after a high school football game, there may be nowhere in Texas that feels as Texas as a Whataburger when you’re not quite ready to call it a night.

One of the defining features of Whataburger has always been its friendliness to customizing your meal—made to order. Want jalapeños and mustard on your burger, no mayo? Go right ahead, sweetie.

On Tuesday night, as part of national rebuke to President Donald Trump’s party, Texas made its choice clear.

#6667. Copycat Coopers Hawk Red Wine–Braised Short Ribs

This copycat Cooper's Hawk red wine-braised short ribs recipe delivers fall-apart-tender short ribs bathed in a luxurious sauce. It's like dining out in your kitchen.

One taste of the red wine–braised short ribs at Cooper’s Hawk is enough to understand why they’ve remained a bestseller. A generous portion of melt-in-your-mouth braised short ribs is stacked over a mound of buttery whipped potatoes, then drizzled with umami-rich braising liquid. When served with roasted vegetables and garnished with crispy fried onion strings, it’s a plate of comfort food that’s just as much a feast for the eyes as it is for the taste buds.

Whether you’ve been to Cooper’s Hawk and want to recreate the magic at home, or you don’t live near a Cooper’s Hawk location and want to know what all the fuss is about, this copycat recipe belongs on your must-try list. It’s the perfect recipe for chilly days when you want a meal that feels like a warm hug. It’s also impressive-looking and great for feeding a crowd, so keep it in mind as the holiday season approaches.

Cooper’s Hawk Winery and Restaurant is something like a more refined Cheesecake Factory that’s known for its wine rather than its cheesecake. Let me break it down. First, each chain greets diners by showcasing its specialties: Where the Cheesecake Factory has cases of cheesecake, Cooper’s Hawk has a well-appointed wine shop. Second, both are known for extensive menus that span a wide range of global influences and cuisines. Finally, both have a long list of signature dishes (we’ve replicated many Cheesecake Factory copycat recipes over the years) that keep customers coming back. These copycat Cooper’s Hawk red wine–braised short ribs, for example, are an ode to the dish that’s been on the menu since the restaurant opened its very first location in 2005.

Preheat the oven to 425°F. Sprinkle the short ribs with salt and pepper. In an ovenproof Dutch oven over medium-high heat, brown the ribs in oil in batches. Remove the meat and set it aside.

Add the celery, carrot and onion to the drippings, and cook them until they’re tender. Add the garlic, and cook for one minute longer. Add the wine and broth, stirring to loosen the browned bits from the pan.

Return the ribs to the pot. Add the parsley and thyme. Cover the pot and transfer it to the preheated oven. Cook the ribs for 2 hours to 2 hours and 30 minutes or until the meat is tender.

While the ribs are braising, in a small bowl, whisk all the butter ingredients until they’re blended. Transfer the mixture to a sheet of storage wrap, and roll it into a log. Refrigerate the butter until it’s chilled. Unwrap and slice it.

Place the hot mashed potatoes on a serving plate. Top them with the short ribs. Immediately top the ribs with a slice of Dijon butter and french-fried onions. Garnish the dish with additional fresh parsley, if desired.

Store any leftover short ribs in an airtight container in the refrigerator. Enjoy them within four days. Leftovers can be microwaved in a microwave-safe container, or they can be transferred to a Dutch oven and warmed in a 350° oven until they’re heated through.

Braised short ribs freeze like a dream. Store them in a freezer-safe airtight container and freeze them for three to four months. Defrost them completely in the refrigerator before warming them in the microwave or in the oven.

Short ribs are a heavily marbled cut of beef from the lower portion of the rib cage (the same area as the chuck and brisket). They have a robust, beefy flavor but contain a lot of connective tissue, so you need to cook them slowly with low heat for the meat to become tender.

Braising is one of the best (and most popular) ways to prepare short ribs. That said, you can make bone-in short ribs in a slow cooker or on a wood, pellet or charcoal smoker. To speed up the process, you can also make tender bone-in short ribs in a pressure cooker.

Cooper’s Hawk serves their short ribs with mashed potatoes and roasted vegetables, but that is far from the only pairing option. Serve them over a bowl of creamy polenta or on a bed of buttered egg noodles (similar to beef Stroganoff). For freshness, add a garden salad, grilled asparagus or creamed spinach for a more indulgent spin.

Sure! If you want to recreate Cooper’s Hawk braised short rib risotto, prepare this recipe as directed, minus the potatoes, veggies, and onion strings. Instead, saute a blend of mushrooms in a skillet and prepare this parmesan risotto while the short ribs braise in the oven. When everything is ready, shred the short ribs into small pieces and combine them with the mushrooms and risotto. Serve the risotto in shallow bowls with a few spoonfuls of braising liquid and a drizzle of white truffle oil.

#6666. Harvest Caesar Salad

Caesar salad is a year-round favorite in my kitchen, but this harvest spin is on repeat during the fall. Butternut squash pieces are baked with crispy baked Parmesan frico, turning them into cheesy squash “croutons” that give this classic salad the perfect autumnal spin. Trust me—it’s the Friendsgiving dish that everyone will be requesting next year.

The kale:Raw kale can be aggressive, with a rough, almost squeaky texture, so it’s important to treat it by massaging it with both lemon juice and salt before tossing with the dressing. The combination of acid and salt (and your elbow grease!) works together to partially break down the kale fibers, tenderizing it. Wondering how you go about “massaging” the kale? It’s not a science: You literally pretend the bowl of greens is someone’s shoulders. Put your hands in there and massage away!

The croutons:Similar to my crispy Parmesan potatoes, these frico squash croutons are made by roasting the squash on a bed of shredded Parm. In the oven, the cheese melts and caramelizes on the baking sheet, forming this crunchy, crispy crust underneath the squash. This isn’t a difficult technique, but there are a few tips that will make the process much easier.

Make ahead:The frico squash croutons are best fresh (once refrigerated, they’ll lose their crispness), but the dressing can be made 1 day ahead. The kale can also be destemmed and torn up to 1 day ahead, but wait to massage it with the lemon juice and salt until just before serving.

#6665. Cranberry and Brie Stuffed Chicken

With its savory spinach filling, fruity sauce and gooey cheese topping, this cranberry Brie chicken makes any day a celebration.

Who doesn’t love a recipe that looks like it took hours in the kitchen, but is actually surprisingly easy to pull off? Our Test Kitchen’s cranberry Brie chicken is one of those impressive dinners. Tender chicken breasts are stuffed with a spinach filling, coated in bread crumbs and baked until golden. Then comes the best part: the cranberry sauce topping and slices of creamy Brie that melt right over the top.

With its festive colors and a blend of sweet and savory flavors, this dish is a great choice for Friendsgiving, Christmas Eve dinner or any occasion you want to impress guests. But don’t save it just for company! It’s also a fun way to dress up chicken breasts during the week.

Preheat the oven to 375°F. In a large skillet, cook the onion in oil until it’s almost tender. Add the spinach and garlic, and cook them until the spinach is wilted. Drain any liquid, if necessary. Season the filling with salt and pepper.

Pound the chicken breasts with a meat mallet to 1/4-inch thickness. Divide the spinach mixture among the pieces. Fold the chicken breasts in half, enclosing the filling, and secure them with toothpicks.

Place the bread crumbs and egg in separate shallow bowls. Dip the stuffed chicken breasts into the egg, then roll them in the crumbs to coat them. Place them seam side down in an 8-inch square baking dish coated with cooking spray. Bake the chicken, uncovered, for 25 minutes.

Spoon the cranberry sauce over the stuffed chicken breasts. Top them with slices of Brie (if desired, remove the rind from the Brie). Bake the chicken, uncovered, for 10 to 15 minutes longer or until a thermometer inserted into the thickest part reads 165°. Discard the toothpicks before serving the chicken. If desired, garnish it with rosemary sprigs.

Let leftover cranberry Brie chicken cool slightly, then transfer it to an airtight container and refrigerate for up to four days. The breading will soften as it sits, especially under the cranberry sauce and melted Brie, but it’ll still be tasty once reheated.

Cranberry Brie chicken tastes best fresh out of the oven, but you can absolutely get a head start on prepping the recipe. Make the spinach filling, and stuff the chicken breasts, securing them with toothpicks. Cover and refrigerate both for up to 24 hours.

When you’re ready to make dinner, dip the chicken in the egg, coat it with bread crumbs and bake it as directed. Save the cranberry sauce and Brie for the last 10 to 15 minutes of baking. Waiting to coat the chicken until just before baking helps keep the bread crumbs from getting soggy.

Reheat cranberry Brie chicken, loosely covered with foil, in a 350° oven until it’s warmed through to 165°. The microwave also works for single servings, but the breading will be a little soggier.

We love Brie here because its mild flavor and creamy texture pair so well with the tart cranberry sauce, but it’s not your only option. Camembert has a similar creamy texture and earthy flavor, or you could use goat cheese if you want something bolder and tangier. For a milder, kid-friendly option, try mozzarella or fontina. Both melt beautifully into a gooey, cheesy topping.

Boneless skinless chicken thighs can work in this recipe, but their smaller size makes them a little trickier to pound thin and fold around the spinach filling. If possible, choose larger thighs, and use toothpicks to keep the filling tucked inside. Since thighs vary in size and thickness, you may need to adjust baking time. Use a meat thermometer to make sure the chicken reaches an internal temperature of 165° before serving it.

Cranberry Brie chicken fits right in with holiday favorites like creamy mashed potatoes, roasted Brussels sprouts, stuffing or green bean casserole. For a more casual weeknight dinner, serve it over hot, fluffy rice to soak up the extra cranberry sauce, or pair it with roasted sweet potatoes or a simple green salad. And you can’t go wrong with a side of crusty bread, warm buttermilk biscuits or cornbread!

Researchers hope recursive self-improvement could tackle the skyrocketing costs of developing advanced AI models. But is it viable?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists in China are exploring what it would take to develop "the last AI built by humans" — a powerful, self-improving artificial intelligence (AI) system capable of creating its own successors.

In a new paper, researchers examine how approaches to recursive self-improvement (RSI) could help tackle the rising financial and computational costs of developing ever-more advanced AI models.

RSI refers to the idea that future AI models could direct their own training and development, using what they learn from each round of improvements to guide subsequent rounds of development.

This recursive feedback loop could eventually enable AI systems to develop newer, more powerful generations of models with minimal human input.

The study, which was uploaded to the preprint database arXiv Sept. 10 but has not been peer-reviewed, proposes a framework for classifying AI systems based on their self-improvement capabilities, from Level 1 (lowest) to Level 5 (highest).

At the lower levels, development remains largely human-led. As AI systems move up the scale, they become increasingly capable of identifying their weaknesses and deciding how to address them, eventually gaining the ability to make their own “meta-improvements” — improving how they improve themselves.

Whether AI could ever achieve this level of sustained self-improvement remains an open question. Previous experiments have, however, demonstrated more limited forms of RSI.

In one study earlier this year, an AI system called A-Evolve-Training was tasked with improving the performance of a 30 billion-parameter large language model (LLM).

Over four rounds, A-Evolve-Training modestly improved the LLM's benchmark performance by testing different training techniques and using the results to change how it approached subsequent experiments.

Peter Bentley, a professor of digital biology at University College London, questioned whether such experiments offer a credible route to RSI.

"This idea that some AI is magically going to start generating better and better AIs by themselves [is] nonsense," Bentley told Live Science in an email.

Bentley pointed out that self-improving computer systems have been around for decades. Evolutionary computation and reinforcement learning, for instance, are both based on the principle of systems refining their performance over time in response to feedback.

Could AI really self-improve? Some experts are skeptical.

The much greater challenge, he said, is developing AI systems capable of autonomously conducting the research needed to create more powerful successors — not to mention overcoming their dependence on human expertise and physical computing infrastructure.

"You can't 'recursively self-improve' unless you can also enhance your own training, enhance your hardware, and test it exhaustively in real world settings," Bentley added.

The study's authors acknowledged some of these challenges. Developing RSI-capable systems could require enormous investments in computing power, as well as human supervision to ensure successive improvements delivered meaningful gains. All of this becomes effectively redundant if the resources needed to develop and test subsequent AI models outweigh any benefits they offer, the authors noted.

Scientists would also need a reliable way to determine whether an AI system was genuinely becoming more capable over iterations, rather than exploiting weaknesses in tests used to measure its capabilities. This is a known problem in AI development, where models can achieve higher benchmark scores by exploiting testing methods or cherry-picking results.

Kayla Blomquist, an AI researcher at the University of Oxford and co-founder of the Oxford China Policy Lab, said that, while the paper doesn't provide a practical road map to RSI, it could help developers and policymakers understand the technical challenges and safety risks associated with increasingly autonomous AI systems.

She also questioned whether there would ever be a clear point at which AI became completely independent of human development. "The paper describes a gradual handover of responsibility rather than a single moment, so there may never be an obvious 'last' model built by humans," Blomquist added.

#6663. Chrissy Teigen Reveals Her Go-To Date Night Food With John Legend—And It’s Surprisingly Simple

Chrissy Teigen and John Legend might be one of Hollywood's most recognizable couples, but apparently, even they struggle to find time for a date night.

On the latest episode of Déjà Food, the cookbook author opens up about her favorite meals with Legend, revealing that between their busy schedules and raising four children, finding time for a night out isn’t always easy. But when they do manage to sneak away, there’s one type of food they almost always gravitate toward.

“We don't often get date nights, but when we do, it's Italian,” Teigen says.

And considering the couple’s history, that actually makes perfect sense.

Italy has played a pretty significant role in their relationship. The two tied the knot in Lake Como in 2013 and returned to the same destination to celebrate their 10th wedding anniversary.

During the interview, Teigen recalls enjoying an Italian feast at their anniversary celebration and reveals that their wedding dinner featured pasta served from a large cheese wheel.

Italian food also seems to be the couple's preferred choice for birthdays. Teigen recalls celebrating one of her birthdays in Italy, where she believes she ate porcini mushroom risotto, which she describes as one of her favorite dishes.

And for Legend's birthday, she organized a dinner with his New York friends at Casa Cipriani.

“I surprised him with his New York friends, and we went to Casa Cipriani and had an incredible meal,” she says. “Everything they have there is incredible.”

Of course, not every date night has been quite so effortless.

Teigen also shares a story about one of the first times she splurged on dinner for Legend early in their relationship. After months of him treating her, she decided it was finally her turn to pick up the check at a restaurant from Chef Daniel Boulud.

But she was so nervous about her card potentially being declined that she brought a large amount of cash and spent the entire meal mentally calculating the bill.

Things got especially stressful when she ordered a margarita that cost approximately $42.

“I was so nervous, but I had enough cash,” she recalls, before admitting that she thinks Legend ended up paying the tip.

Thankfully, their restaurant dates seem to have become a little less stressful over the years.

And while the couple clearly appreciates an elaborate Italian dinner, Teigen also reveals that Legend recently made her a Kirkland Signature Costco Chicken Bake at home.

“It was like a Hot Pocket, but huge,” she says.

So apparently, the secret to keeping date night interesting is a little Italian food, an occasional fancy restaurant, and sometimes a really big Costco Chicken Bake.

#6662. This Genius Trick Makes Perfectly Portioned Cinnamon Rolls—No Ruler or Guessing Required

This clever little move turns your knife into a measuring guide for cinnamon rolls.

I have no objection to a shortcut in the kitchen. I’m happy to let boxed cake mix handle dessert or a great jar of pasta sauce get dinner moving. But I just can’t make peace with cinnamon rolls from a can. I want to love them. I appreciate the convenience, and I understand the appeal of having warm cinnamon rolls before the coffee is finished brewing. They just never quite satisfy that craving for a warm, deliciously gooey cinnamon roll.

Some viral upgrades make a compelling case—particularly the heavy cream bath and generous additions of butter and brown sugar. But my long-standing love for cinnamon rolls has much more to do with the soft, pillowy dough, so I’m willing to wait through a rise or two.

Having committed to that, though, I’m still interested in anything that makes the process easier. So when I saw a video of someone flipping a knife over a log of cinnamon roll dough to mark perfectly even portions, I wanted to try it. Cutting equal slices by eye can involve a surprising amount of second-guessing when you’d really just like to get them in the pan. I made our classic cinnamon roll recipe and put the trick to the test.

The clever part of this trick is that the knife becomes its own measurement. Rather than judging the thickness of each slice, you use the width of the blade to mark equal portions along the dough roll before slicing it into pieces.

Once your dough is filled and rolled into a log, gently lay the blade flat across the top at one end, with the knife running crosswise over the log. Then flip it onto its opposite flat side, moving along the dough one blade-width at a time. It looks a little like the knife is doing small somersaults, with its edge leaving a light indentation at each turn.

Continue down the log, using just enough pressure to leave visible marks. Then go back and slice through the dough at those marks.

This worked beautifully with our classic cinnamon rolls, but the same technique would work with just about any cinnamon roll recipe. The turning motion was simple, and the knife left an evenly spaced cutting guide along the dough. Once the marks were there, I could slice the rolls without measuring each one or estimating where the next cut should go.

I particularly liked being able to see all the portions before I started cutting. It made the job feel settled: The spacing was already worked out, and all I had to do was follow it. For something that takes so little effort, it’s a useful bit of precision.

This is the kind of cinnamon roll shortcut I can get behind. I still get the homemade rolls I wanted, but there’s one less thing to fuss over before the pan goes into the oven.

#6660. Collard Greens Vinaigrette

For those who might shudder at the thought of eating raw hardy greens like collards or kale, this vibrant side inspired by the French bistro classic leeks vinaigrette is the answer. Simmered past squeaky-raw yet well short of meltingly braised, they offer substantial bite, like al dente pasta. The mustard dressing couldn’t be simpler to make—use it as a base for any salad you might serve this season. It’s punchy enough to stand up to winter vegetables or any sturdy bitter green.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Toast ½ cup raw walnuts on a rimmed baking sheet, tossing halfway through, until golden brown, 10–12 minutes.

Meanwhile, cook 2 bunches collard greens, ribs and stems removed, leaves cut into 2" pieces, in a large pot of generously salted boiling water until just tender, 9–11 minutes. Using tongs, immediately transfer to a large bowl of ice water and let cool.

Whisk 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, ¼ cup white wine vinegar, 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, preferably country-style, ⅓ cup extra-virgin olive oil, ¼ cup (packed) coarsely chopped tarragon, 2 tsp. sugar, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl to combine. Set dressing aside.

Transfer toasted walnuts to a small bowl and drizzle with remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Sprinkle with a generous pinch each of sugar and salt and toss to coat. Taste and add more sugar if needed (nuts should be more sweet than salty). Set seasoned walnuts aside.

Drain collard greens and squeeze gently to remove excess water. Transfer to bowl with reserved dressing and toss to coat evenly. Cover and chill at least 15 minutes and up to 2 hours.

Arrange greens in a shallow bowl or on a platter and spoon any dressing remaining in bowl over. Top with seasoned walnuts and tarragon leaves.

Do Ahead: Walnuts can be toasted and dressing can be made 1 day ahead. Store walnuts airtight at room temperature. Cover dressing and chill.

#6659. Sweet Potato Crème Brûlée Bars

Let them chill:For the best results, make these bars a day in advance to give them enough chill time for perfectly cut squares. This will help bond and blend your batter together more easily, resulting in a homogeneous and smooth batter.

Make ahead:The bars can be made and refrigerated 2 days ahead of time or frozen in an airtight container for up to 2 months without the topping. To thaw, take the bars out of the freezer and leave them in the refrigerator overnight. Brûlée the topping just before serving.
